kurz: Who decides on the distribution, how it changes the balance sheet, and under what condition a retained euro is worth more than one paid out.

bloecke.md:
A public limited company (AG) does not distribute the profit reported in the press. What is distributed is the **distributable profit** (Bilanzgewinn), and it only emerges after three calculation steps that follow net profit for the year. First, 5% of net profit for the year, reduced by any loss carryforward, must be transferred to the legal reserve until this reserve, together with the capital reserve, reaches 10% of the share capital (Section 150 AktG (Stock Corporation Act)). Second, when adopting the annual financial statements, the management board and supervisory board may transfer up to half of net profit for the year to other revenue reserves (Section 58(2) AktG). This money stays in the company without the owners being asked. Third, any profit carryforward from the previous year is added, or any loss carryforward is deducted.

The [[Annual general meeting (AGM)|annual general meeting]] decides only on the remaining amount (Section 174(1) AktG), and in doing so it is bound by the adopted annual financial statements. Information on the distribution of a German group therefore comes from the statement of appropriation of profit and not from the profit line.

bloecke.titel: From net profit to the amount distributed
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in € million; the legal reserve is already fully funded. The management board and supervisory board transfer 480 of the 1,200 million profit to other revenue reserves; with the profit carryforward of 60 million, 780 million is available for distribution.

bloecke.md:
## Resolution, due date and ex-dividend date

The annual general meeting can amend the proposal of the management board and supervisory board, but only within the limits of the distributable profit. The resolution gives rise to the individual shareholder's claim to payment. It falls due on the third business day following the annual general meeting (Section 58(4) sentence 2 AktG). As early as the first trading day after the annual general meeting, the share trades without this claim. This day is called the ex-dividend date.

On the ex-dividend date, the share opens lower by the amount of the dividend resolved, as a matter of arithmetic. The [[Ex-dividend markdown|ex-dividend markdown]] is not an assessment by the market; it follows arithmetically from the fact that from this day on the buyer acquires one claim less. Derivatives exchanges and index providers take this markdown into account in their calculations. Empirically, the price falls on average by slightly less than the full dividend. The causes, such as different tax rates among groups of investors and trading costs, have been debated for decades. The direction, by contrast, is clear: a price markdown on the ex-dividend date is the rule.

A dividend is not a return that the company generates. It is a disposal of wealth that has already been earned and shifts capital from the company's balance sheet into the shareholder's portfolio, where tax is due immediately. The return on a share arises in the income statement and not only on the payment date.

## Effect of the payout on the balance sheet

The payout is a balance sheet contraction. On the assets side, cash and cash equivalents fall, and on the equity and liabilities side, equity falls, both by the same amount, and the balance sheet total becomes smaller. This results in two effects that are regularly overlooked in ratio comparisons. The [[Equity ratio|equity ratio]] falls, although the company has not taken on any debt. [[Return on equity (ROE)|ROE]] rises because the same profit is related to a smaller equity base. This is purely a denominator effect without any operational improvement. A share buyback of the same size has exactly the same effect, because it also reduces cash and equity by the same amount.

bloecke.titel: Equity and liabilities before and after the distribution
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in € million. Equity falls by the 660 million paid out, liabilities remain unchanged, and the balance sheet total falls from 15,000 to 14,340.

bloecke.md:
## Distributions and the owners' wealth

Suppose two companies have the same business, the same risk and the same profit. One distributes its profit, the other retains it. As long as the retained money earns the return that the owner would demand on the capital market for this risk, the owner is equally wealthy in both cases. This is the central statement of Miller and Modigliani's irrelevance theorem from 1961. It holds exactly only in a world without taxes and transaction costs.

In Germany, both exist. Above all, however, the condition of “the same return” is not automatically met. Whether retention benefits or harms the owner depends on it.

bloecke.erklaerung: The sustainable growth rate is the rate at which a company can grow from its own resources without issuing new shares or increasing its debt-to-equity ratio. Every retained euro increases equity, and the return on equity is earned again on the enlarged equity in the following year.
variablen: sustainable growth rate of profit and equity per year
net profit divided by average equity
bloecke.beispiel: ROE 18%, payout ratio 55% → g = 18 × 0.45 = 8.1%. If the ratio is raised to 80%, g falls to 3.6%. The higher dividend therefore comes at the expense of future growth.

bloecke.unter: Calculated using g = ROE × (1 − payout ratio), not a forecast. With a 20% return on equity, the same payout ratio costs twice as much growth as with 10%.

bloecke.md: Whether this trade-off pays off depends solely on the relationship between return on equity and cost of equity. The KPMG Cost of Capital Study finds an average cost of equity of 9.7% for companies from Germany, Austria and Switzerland, with a WACC of 8.5%. The sample covers around 300 companies, including about two thirds of the DAX 40. Combining this required return r with the sustainable growth rate g gives a rule-of-thumb formula for the price-to-book ratio. It originally comes from bank valuation but can be applied generally: P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (r − g).

bloecke.titel: Payout ratio and theoretical P/B ratio at a 9.7% cost of equity

bloecke.md: If a company earns roughly its cost of capital, the table shows that payout policy has hardly any effect. The price-to-book ratio then stays close to one, however the profit is distributed. Only a lasting gap between ROE and the cost of capital makes retention valuable and distribution expensive. At the same time, the formula shows its limit. As g approaches r, the quotient becomes very large, and if g is above r, it no longer gives a meaningful value. No company can permanently grow faster than the return its owners require. Valuations based on such values therefore only reflect an assumption and not a forecast.

## Payout ratio

A [[Payout ratio|payout ratio]] contains more information than any yield figure, because it does not depend on the share price. However, it has two possible denominators, and only the two together give a complete picture. Relative to net profit, it measures what share of accounting profit is handed over. Relative to [[Free cash flow|free cash flow]], it measures whether the money for the distribution was actually there. Net profit contains non-cash items such as depreciation, provisions and write-ups, whereas the dividend is paid out by bank transfer.

bloecke.titel: Three model companies with the same dividend

bloecke.md: With a ratio of 50% to profit, company B looks cautious, but it pays out 40 million more than the business generates in free cash flow and is already more heavily indebted. With 139%, company C looks worrying. However, its profit probably includes a non-cash write-down, and the dividend is well covered by cash flow. If, on the other hand, both ratios are permanently above 100%, the distribution is being financed from cash, from asset sales or through borrowing. A dividend paid on credit cannot be sustained permanently and will foreseeably be cut.

## Dividend aristocrats

The S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats only includes companies that have raised their dividend for at least 25 consecutive years. The European version requires ten years of stable or rising distributions. Membership is therefore determined in hindsight, and today's members are included because they have stayed the course. The index curve, on the other hand, is based on the composition at each point in time. Companies that later dropped out are included in it up to the point of their exit. However, values before the index was launched in May 2005 are back-calculated, and according to S&P such back-calculations can benefit from knowledge of subsequent developments.

Companies that fail leave the list after the cut and disappear from the ongoing statistics. General Electric had raised its dividend for over three decades and cut it in February 2009 from 31 to 10 US cents per quarter. It was the first cut since 1938. Bayer cut its distribution for the 2023 financial year to €0.11 per share, after the group had been regarded as a reliable payer for years. In spring 2020, several DAX companies cut their dividends, and some, such as Adidas and Lufthansa, scrapped them altogether. A long track record points to a stable business but does not guarantee future payments. Such a streak is usually broken just when investors would need the money most.

## Taxation of dividends from individual shares

Dividends are income from capital assets (Section 20(1) no. 1 EStG (Income Tax Act)). The paying agent withholds 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge (Sections 43, 43a EStG), 26.375% in total, or around 28% with church tax. The only deduction allowed is the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG). Individually documented income-related expenses (Werbungskosten) are not deductible. Unlike with funds, there is no partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) for shares held directly, because the 30% under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) only applies to units in equity funds. The partial exemption, however, compensates on a flat-rate basis for the fact that the fund itself already bears taxes: 15% capital income withholding tax on German dividends (Sections 6, 7 InvStG), and on foreign dividends the withholding tax that the investor cannot credit. For a German dividend, the total burden via an equity fund is around 30.7%, compared with 26.375% for a direct holding. For foreign shares held directly, withholding tax comes on top. It is only credited up to the rate provided for in the double taxation agreement (Section 32d(5) EStG).

bloecke.titel: Distributions from the tax contribution account
bloecke.md:
If a company makes a distribution from the tax contribution account (steuerliches Einlagekonto) under Section 27 KStG (Corporation Tax Act), the money comes from capital contributed earlier instead of from taxed profits. Such amounts do not count as income within the meaning of Section 20(1) no. 1 EStG and are received without capital income withholding tax.

In return, they reduce the acquisition cost of the share. An investor who bought the share for €40 and has received €6 in this way over the years uses an acquisition cost of €34 when selling. The tax is therefore payable later, on a correspondingly larger capital gain. Some German groups have paid their dividends this way for several years. Which part was affected is stated in the bank's tax certificate and in the company's certificate.

## Buyback and dividend compared

A [[Share buyback|share buyback]] also returns capital to the owners, but distributes it only to the shareholders who sell. The annual general meeting must authorise the management board to do so, for at most five years and for at most 10% of the share capital (Section 71(1) no. 8 AktG). Shareholders who do not sell receive no money. Afterwards, they hold a larger stake in the same company. The following calculation keeps profit and the amount paid out constant and shows only what the form of the return changes.

bloecke.titel: €100 million returned to the owners (illustrative calculation)

bloecke.md:
In both cases, the market value of equity falls by exactly the 100 million paid out, and the price-to-earnings ratio is 11.25 afterwards in each case. The higher earnings per share after the buyback create no new value, because the same profit is simply spread over fewer shares.

The difference of €26.38 per €1,000 of portfolio value is also a deferred tax, not a saved one. The acquisition cost remains unchanged, and the tax on the capital gain becomes due on sale. The deferral is nevertheless worth a lot, because the amount remains invested until then and generates income. In addition, you can choose the timing yourself, for example a year with low other income in which the most-favourable assessment (Günstigerprüfung) under Section 32d(6) EStG pays off.

On the other side are the drawbacks of a buyback. A dividend is a visible promise that management boards are reluctant to break. A buyback programme, by contrast, is a declaration of intent that can expire without attracting attention. In addition, a buyback only has an effect if the share count falls over several years. What matters, therefore, is the number of shares outstanding in the notes to the accounts, not the press release about the announced volume.

- Read from the statement of appropriation of profit how large the distributable profit was and how much had been transferred to reserves before the annual general meeting could decide.
- Place both ratios side by side over five years, that is, the dividend divided by net profit and divided by free cash flow.
- Compare the return on equity with the cost of capital. If it is clearly and permanently above the roughly 9% to 10% that equity costs on average in Germany, retention is valuable. If it is below, distribution is the more sensible use.
- Check whether the share count has fallen, risen or stayed the same over five years. This one line says more than most buyback announcements.

mitnehmen: What is distributed is the distributable profit and not net profit for the year. The management board and supervisory board may retain up to half of the profit in advance (Section 58(2) AktG); only the rest is decided on by the annual general meeting.
The payout contracts the balance sheet. The equity ratio falls and ROE rises without anything changing operationally.
According to g = ROE × (1 − payout ratio), every percentage point paid out costs growth. Whether this is worthwhile depends solely on the gap between return on equity and cost of equity.
A payout ratio needs two denominators. The ratio to profit shows the accounting view; the ratio to free cash flow shows whether the money was there.
Dividends and buybacks reduce the value of the company by the same amount. They differ in the timing of the tax, in how binding they are and in who receives the money.

begriffe.text: The amount available for distribution at an AG. It is calculated as net profit for the year plus profit carryforward, less loss carryforward and transfers to the legal reserve and other revenue reserves. The annual general meeting votes only on this amount (Section 174 AktG).
The growth rate that a company can achieve from its own resources, without new shares and without higher debt. It is calculated as g = ROE × (1 − payout ratio).
Dividend divided by free cash flow. It shows whether the distribution is covered by the current cash surplus. The ratio to profit does not show this, because profit contains non-cash items.

Account under Section 27 KStG in which contributed capital outside the share capital is recorded. Distributions from it are not capital income but reduce the acquisition cost of the share. This defers the tax until the sale.
